title: Invidens Sappho: How They Made the Tenth Muse Illiterate and Jealous
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: A reception history of how the jealousy reading of Sappho fragment 31 was made and kept. Antiquity holds the maker and authority on love, the lover who loses, and the poem's detached body apart, and no seated ancient witness joins the lover to the poem through jealousy. The modern record shows the reading made by acts of different kinds, each read at its page: Hermann's declared conjecture of 1816 ('refinxi') and the conditional reading he drew from it, Welcker's refusal of it by name, Mure's rival given as the scene (1850), Bergk's apparatus, Smyth's denial, Page's declared amendment authorized by an account of antiquity (1955), and present-day headings, introductions and classrooms that name the emotion before the poem. Closure of the text and closure of the reading are separate operations, and the reading survives a marked text and a quoted objection. The same reception took the poet's hand: antiquity shows her reading and writing, and she is received as a voice overwhelmed. The findings are read under the sophistry measure (#1727).

wiki_article: Invidens Sappho: How They Made the Tenth Muse Illiterate and Jealous is a reception history by Lee Sharks, deposited on 8 November 2026 in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics as the companion of Closing the Fragment (#1749). It follows how the jealousy reading of Sappho fragment 31 was made and kept. It reads antiquity first: the maker and authority on love in Plato, Strabo, Longinus, Plutarch and Maximus of Tyre, who calls her love the erotic art of Socrates; the lover who loses in Menander's leap and Ovid's Heroides 15; the poem's symptoms circulating without her in Lucretius, Horace, Theocritus and the physician's story of Stratonice; and the historians Aelian and Athenaeus, who make the lover of Phaon a second Sappho. No seated ancient witness joins the lover to the poem through jealousy. The modern record is read in date order with no line of descent assumed: Gottfried Hermann's Elementa doctrinae metricae of 1816, which declares a refashioned close ('refinxi') and reads envy off it under a conditional; F. G. Welcker's refusal of Hermann by name the same year; William Mure's rival given as the scene in 1850; Bergk's apparatus of 1882; Smyth's denial of 1900; Wilamowitz's wedding song; and Denys Page's declared amendment of the ancient description to 'a love in jealousy', authorized by an account of antiquity that files disagreement as one generation's mistake. A section on the present, 'Jealousy before reading', reads headings, a radio introduction, a sixth-grade class and essays that name the emotion before the poem, and finds that closure of the text and closure of the reading are separate operations: the reading survives a marked text and a quoted objection. The study also finds that the same reception took the poet's hand, receiving as a voice overwhelmed the poet whom a fifth-century Attic vase shows reading from a roll and whom Ovid made write. Its findings are read under the archive's sophistry measure (#1727), with Hermann's declared conjecture as the control. It carries an SPXI packet and states the priority of the jealousy reading, and the routes between its witnesses, as open.
